display.text: A relationship between two categorical variables, explored by comparing response-category proportions across explanatory groups. Role-type notation: C→C.
A relationship in which categories of the explanatory variable define groups whose quantitative response distributions or means are compared. Role-type notation: C→Q.
A collection of observations grouped closely together and separated from other groups in a scatterplot.
A cell count divided by its column total and multiplied by 100; used for within-group comparisons when the explanatory groups occupy columns.
A percentage calculated within one specified group, using that group's total as the denominator rather than the entire sample size.
A table containing the correlations between pairs of quantitative variables, used to summarize their linear associations.
A relationship whose scatterplot points follow a curved pattern rather than a straight line.
Numerical summaries used to describe the observed distributions, such as the summaries accompanying comparisons of groups.
The variable used to explain or predict the response. Calling a variable explanatory does not by itself establish a causal effect. Also called the independent variable, denoted X.
The overall shape of the pattern relating two quantitative variables, such as a line or curve.
Samples from separate groups with no observation-by-observation pairing; the two sample sizes need not be equal.
A relationship whose scatterplot points lie approximately around a straight line.
Two sets of measurements linked in pairs, either from the same individuals measured twice or from individuals matched in a relevant way. Matched pairs are a form of dependent samples.
An association in which larger values of one variable tend to occur with smaller values of the other.
An association in which larger values of one variable tend to occur with larger values of the other.
A relationship in which a numerical explanatory variable is used to explain or predict a categorical outcome. Role-type notation: Q→C.
A relationship between two numerical variables, explored by plotting paired values and examining how the response changes with the explanatory variable. Role-type notation: Q→Q.
The outcome whose variation a study seeks to explain or predict. Also called the dependent variable, denoted Y.
A cell count divided by its row total and multiplied by 100; used for within-group comparisons when the explanatory groups occupy rows.
A graph in which each point represents an individual's paired quantitative values, with the explanatory variable on the horizontal axis and the response on the vertical axis.
Boxplots displayed on a common quantitative scale to compare a response distribution across categories of an explanatory variable.
How closely observations follow the relationship's overall form; stronger relationships have less scatter around that pattern.
The plan for selecting individuals and obtaining measurements, including whether comparisons use independent groups or matched pairs.
A group within a population defined by a characteristic, such as one category of an explanatory variable.
The population average of the quantitative response for the group defined by category i of an explanatory variable. Notation: μᵢ.
A table that cross-classifies two categorical variables, with each cell counting observations in a particular combination of categories. Also called cross table.
